statements.text: If they come in and disable the code that runs that military equipment, it's unclear what happens. [...] do we need some kind of a Geneva Convention for cyber warfare? [...] we can control our AI, but if China or Russia does something differently, we're beyond the pale. Should we be thinking more about international law in this context?
statements.context: House Science Committee hearing on open-source software cybersecurity, where Rep. Casten poses a question to a witness about international cyber rules.

statements.text: And as you think about how to create an ecosystem that provides trusted AI resources, do you think this is an ecosystem design problem or somebody actually going in and designing the—does that metaphor hold up?
statements.context: House subcommittee hearing on open-source software cybersecurity, where Rep. Casten poses a question to a testifying expert about AI resource governance.

statements.text: I ask because there has been some reporting of private sector actors who are now using AI to do it. [...] to the extent those models are using the same datasets that your models are using, that would seem to be mutually beneficial for compliance. To the extent they are different, it would seem to create headaches.
statements.context: House financial services hearing on leveraging technology in financial services.

statements.text: The Chair has warned the financial institutions that they are going to rely on a limited number of AI platforms, but I think he has been very open, and I think very thoughtful, about saying that your regulation is at the level of a given entity, but if those entities are now relying on a single set of cross-company platforms, if the problem is with that platform, do you all have the tools to assess these questions? Do you need help from Congress? How are you thinking about this question, if there is dataset integrity, from ethics or otherwise, and it spans a lot of different companies?
statements.context: Casten questions financial regulators during a House Financial Services Committee hearing on technology in financial services.

statements.text: And are you making public what datasets you are using to train the AI?
statements.context: Congressional hearing on financial innovation, where Rep. Casten questions a witness about AI training data transparency.

statements.text: do any of you currently have in that code blocks that test for disparate treatment or for disparate impact?
statements.context: House Financial Services Committee hearing on AI applications in financial services and housing, where Rep. Casten questions industry panelists about bias testing.

statements.text: I have this growing concern that you see a lot of people saying, well, the AI did it, I did not do it, I did not program it to do this.
statements.context: Congressional hearing of the House Financial Services Committee's AI Working Group on AI applications in financial services and housing.

statements.text: you would also like to build an AI data center in China to train the algorithm that is needed for your autonomous vehicles. That sure sounds like something that would also probably be restricted given the data collection.
statements.context: House hearing examining policies to counter China, where Rep. Casten questions a witness about their AI and data operations in China.

statements.text: In practice, we have an entire industry saying I want complete absolution of any liability from any of my AI models. In fact, all of our Republican colleagues just voted last week to pass a piece of legislation that says, there shall be no liability for anybody using the AI model.
statements.context: House Financial Services Committee hearing on data privacy in the financial system.

statements.text: I do not think this is as big a deal as we talk about it. I think we use words—you know, we call it intelligence, but it is just—it is a massive correlation machine. It is not intelligent, per se, but I can plug in huge amounts of data on the markets and historic trading trends, and say I want this algorithm using those historic correlations to identify relationships and optimize for profit margin. It can do that. It is really cool, right? I can plug in the entire Taylor Swift catalog and say put let us take a Tom Waits song and make it sound like a Taylor Swift song. I can do that. It is not intelligent. It is just massively correlative.
statements.context: Casten questions a witness at a hearing on AI innovation in financial services about federal preemption of state AI laws.
